imo-1993-01.title: Evaluate the factor at $-5$
imo-1993-01.body:
Suppose $f=gh$ with $g,h\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ nonconstant. As $f$ is monic, the leading coefficients of $g,h$ are both $1$ or both $-1$; replacing $g,h$ by $-g,-h$ we may assume both are monic. From $g(0)h(0)=f(0)=3$, one of them, say $g$, has $|g(0)|=1$. Let $k=\deg g\ge1$ and let $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k$ be the complex roots of $g$, so $g(x)=\prod_i(x-\alpha_i)$ and $\prod_i|\alpha_i|=|g(0)|=1$.

**Each root is a root of $f$:** $\alpha_i^{n-1}(\alpha_i+5)=-3$. Taking absolute values and multiplying over $i$,
$$\Big(\prod_i|\alpha_i|\Big)^{n-1}\prod_i|\alpha_i+5|=3^k,\qquad\text{so}\qquad \prod_i|\alpha_i+5|=3^k.$$
But $\prod_i(\alpha_i+5)=\prod_i(-1)(-5-\alpha_i)=(-1)^kg(-5)$, hence $|g(-5)|=3^k$.

**On the other hand** $g(-5)\,h(-5)=f(-5)=(-5)^n+5(-5)^{n-1}+3=3$, with $h(-5)$ an integer, so $|g(-5)|$ divides $3$. Therefore $3^k\le3$, i.e. $k=1$, and $g(x)=x-\alpha_1$ with $\alpha_1=\pm1$ (since $|g(0)|=1$). So $f(1)=0$ or $f(-1)=0$.

But $f(1)=9$ and $f(-1)=(-1)^n+5(-1)^{n-1}+3=3-4(-1)^n\in\{-1,7\}$, neither zero. Contradiction. ∎

imo-1993-02.title: Complex numbers for (a), tangent–chord angles for (b)
imo-1993-02.body:
**(a)** Place $C$ at the origin of the complex plane and let $a,b,d$ be the complex numbers of $A,B,D$. Orient the plane so that rotating $\overrightarrow{CB}$ counterclockwise by $\angle ACB$ gives the direction of $\overrightarrow{CA}$, i.e. $\arg\frac ab=\angle ACB$. Since $D$ lies on the same side of $AB$ as $C$, triangles $CBA$ and $DBA$ have the same orientation, so $\arg\frac{a-d}{b-d}=\angle ADB$.

Put $u=a(b-d)$ and $v=b(a-d)$. Then
$$|u|=AC\cdot BD=AD\cdot BC=|v|,\qquad \arg\frac uv=\arg\frac ab-\arg\frac{a-d}{b-d}=\angle ACB-\angle ADB=-90^\circ .$$
So $u=-i\,v$. Now
$$u-v=ab-ad-ab+bd=d(b-a),\qquad |u-v|=|-i-1|\,|v|=\sqrt2\,|v| .$$
Since $|d(b-a)|=CD\cdot AB$ and $|v|=AD\cdot BC=AC\cdot BD$, we get
$$\frac{AB\cdot CD}{AC\cdot BD}=\sqrt2 .$$

**(b)** First, since $D$ is inside the triangle,
$$\angle ADB=360^\circ-\angle ADC-\angle BDC=(\angle CAD+\angle ACD)+(\angle CBD+\angle BCD)=\angle CAD+\angle CBD+\angle ACB,$$
using the angle sums of triangles $ACD$ and $BCD$. With the hypothesis, $\angle CAD+\angle CBD=90^\circ$.

Let $t_1$ be the tangent at $C$ to circle $ACD$. By the tangent–chord theorem, the ray $r_1$ of $t_1$ on the side of line $CD$ opposite to $A$ makes the angle $\angle CAD$ with ray $CD$. Likewise the ray $r_2$ of the tangent $t_2$ to circle $BCD$ on the side opposite to $B$ makes the angle $\angle CBD$ with ray $CD$. The line $CD$ separates $A$ from $B$ ($D$ is inside the triangle), so $r_1$ lies on $B$'s side and $r_2$ on $A$'s side: the rays $r_1$ and $r_2$ are on opposite sides of ray $CD$, and
$$\angle(r_1,r_2)=\angle CAD+\angle CBD=90^\circ .$$
So the two tangents are perpendicular. ∎

**Answer:** (a) $\sqrt2$.

imo-1993-03.title: 3-colouring invariant and a strip-removal gadget
imo-1993-03.body:
Use coordinates (row, column).

## $3\mid n$ is impossible

Give square $(x,y)$ the colour $x+y\bmod 3$. Any three consecutive squares in a row or column have three different colours. A move empties two of them (the jumping piece's square and the jumped one) and fills the third, so each of the three colour counts changes by exactly $1$: all three parities flip together. If $3\mid n$, each colour initially occupies $n^2/3$ squares, so the three counts always have equal parity. A single remaining piece gives counts $1,0,0$ — not all of the same parity. So the game cannot end with one piece.

## $3\nmid n$ is possible

**Gadget.** Suppose the squares $X_1,X_2,X_3$ of a $1\times3$ strip are occupied, $H$ is an occupied square adjacent to the end square $X_1$ in the direction perpendicular to the strip, and the square $O$ on the other side of $X_1$ (so $H,X_1,O$ are in a line) is empty. Then: $H$ jumps over $X_1$ to $O$; $X_3$ jumps over $X_2$ to $X_1$; the piece on $O$ jumps over $X_1$ back to $H$. Net effect: the strip is emptied and nothing else changes.

**Lemma.** An $a\times b$ block (rows $1..a$, columns $1..b$) with $a\ge3$, $b\ge4$ can be reduced to the $a\times(b-3)$ block of its first $b-3$ columns.

*Proof.* For $r=1,2,\dots,a-3$ remove the strip $(r,b-2),(r,b-1),(r,b)$ using $X_1=(r,b)$, $H=(r+1,b)$, $O=(r-1,b)$ ($O$ is outside the block or already emptied). Then for $c=b,b-1,b-2$ remove the vertical strip $(a-2,c),(a-1,c),(a,c)$ using $X_1=(a-2,c)$, $H=(a-2,c-1)$, $O=(a-2,c+1)$ (again $O$ is empty; for $c=b-2$ the helper is in column $b-3\ge1$). $\square$

By reflecting in the diagonal, an $a\times b$ block with $a\ge4$, $b\ge3$ can be reduced to its top $(a-3)\times b$ block.

**Reduction.** For $N\ge6$: reduce $N\times N$ to $N\times(N-3)$ (Lemma, $a=N\ge3$, $b=N\ge4$), then to $(N-3)\times(N-3)$ (reflected Lemma, $a=N\ge4$, $b=N-3\ge3$). So if $3\nmid n$, an $n\times n$ block reduces to a $1\times1$, $2\times2$, $4\times4$ or $5\times5$ block. These are finished as follows (squares $(r,c)$ with the block in rows and columns $1..n$; "$P\to P'$" means the piece on $P$ jumps to $P'$):
- $n=1$: done.
- $n=2$: $(1,1)\to(1,3)$, $(2,1)\to(2,3)$, $(1,3)\to(3,3)$.
- $n=4$: $(1,2)\to(1,0)$, $(1,3)\to(1,5)$, $(2,2)\to(2,0)$, $(1,0)\to(3,0)$, $(2,3)\to(2,5)$, $(1,5)\to(3,5)$, $(3,1)\to(5,1)$, $(4,3)\to(4,1)$, $(4,4)\to(2,4)$, $(3,2)\to(3,4)$, $(3,5)\to(3,3)$, $(5,1)\to(3,1)$, $(3,0)\to(3,2)$, $(3,2)\to(3,4)$, $(2,4)\to(4,4)$ — one piece remains at $(4,4)$.
- $n=5$: use the reflected Lemma ($a=b=5$) to clear rows $3$–$5$, leaving the $2\times5$ block in rows $1,2$; then $(1,1)\to(3,1)$, $(1,2)\to(3,2)$, $(1,3)\to(3,3)$, $(1,5)\to(1,3)$, $(2,5)\to(2,3)$, $(3,2)\to(3,4)$, $(1,3)\to(3,3)$, $(3,4)\to(3,2)$, $(3,1)\to(3,3)$ — one piece remains at $(3,3)$.

**Answer:** the game can end with one piece exactly when $n$ is not divisible by $3$. ∎

imo-1993-04.title: Areas, longest sides and monotonicity
imo-1993-04.body:
For a non-degenerate triangle $T$ with area $[T]$ and longest side $L(T)$, the smallest altitude is the one onto the longest side: $m(T)=\dfrac{2[T]}{L(T)}$ (also true, as $0$, for degenerate $T$). We may assume $A,B,C$ are not collinear.

**Lemma 1.** A segment contained in a triangle is at most as long as the triangle's longest side.
*Proof.* For fixed $Q$ the function $P\mapsto|PQ|$ is convex, so over the triangle it is maximal at a vertex $V$; then $Q\mapsto|VQ|$ is maximal at a vertex $W$, and $|VW|\le L$. $\square$

**Lemma 2.** If triangle $T$ lies in a strip of width $w$, then $m(T)\le w$. In particular, if $T\subseteq T'$ then $m(T)\le m(T')$ (take the strip between the longest side of $T'$ and the parallel through the opposite vertex, of width $m(T')$).
*Proof.* Let $Q$ be the vertex of $T$ whose distance across the strip is in the middle. The line through $Q$ parallel to the strip meets the opposite side at $Q'$ and splits $T$ into two triangles with common base $QQ'$ and heights $h_1,h_2$, $h_1+h_2\le w$. So $[T]=\frac12|QQ'|(h_1+h_2)\le\frac12L(T)\,w$ by Lemma 1, i.e. $m(T)\le w$. $\square$

**Case 1: $X$ lies in the closed triangle $ABC$.** Then $[ABX]+[AXC]+[XBC]=[ABC]$, and every side of the three small triangles lies in $ABC$, so is $\le L=L(ABC)$ by Lemma 1. Hence
$$m(ABX)+m(AXC)+m(XBC)\ge\frac{2[ABX]+2[AXC]+2[XBC]}{L}=\frac{2[ABC]}{L}=m(ABC).$$

**Case 2: $X$ lies outside triangle $ABC$.** Look at the convex hull of $A,B,C,X$.
- If it is a triangle, it must be one of $XBC$, $AXC$, $ABX$ containing the remaining point; say $A\in XBC$. Then $ABC\subseteq XBC$ and Lemma 2 gives $m(ABC)\le m(XBC)$.
- If it is a convex quadrilateral, $X$ is opposite one of $A,B,C$, say $A$ (the quadrilateral is $ABXC$). Its diagonals $AX$ and $BC$ meet at a point $P$ on both segments. By Case 1 applied to $P\in BC$: $m(ABC)\le m(ABP)+m(APC)+m(PBC)=m(ABP)+m(APC)$ ($PBC$ is degenerate). Since $P$ is on segment $AX$, $ABP\subseteq ABX$ and $APC\subseteq AXC$, so by Lemma 2, $m(ABC)\le m(ABX)+m(AXC)$.

The other choices of labels are symmetric (the right-hand side is symmetric in $A,B,C$). In all cases the inequality holds. ∎

imo-1993-05.title: Round $n\varphi$ to the nearest integer
imo-1993-05.body:
Yes. Let $\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$, so $\varphi^2=\varphi+1$ and $\varphi-1=\frac1\varphi$. Define
$$f(n)=\Big\lfloor \varphi n+\tfrac12\Big\rfloor,$$
the integer nearest to $\varphi n$. Since $\varphi n$ is irrational for $n\ge1$, $|f(n)-\varphi n|<\frac12$.

- $f(1)=\lfloor1.618\ldots+0.5\rfloor=2$.
- **Increasing:** $\varphi(n+1)+\frac12-(\varphi n+\frac12)=\varphi>1$, so the floor strictly increases. Also $f(n)\ge f(1)\ge1$, so $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$.
- **$f(f(n))=f(n)+n$:** let $m=f(n)$. Then
$$\varphi m-(m+n)=(\varphi-1)m-n=\frac{m}{\varphi}-n=\frac{m-\varphi n}{\varphi},$$
so $|\varphi m-(m+n)|<\frac{1}{2\varphi}<\frac12$. Hence $m+n$ is the integer nearest to $\varphi m$, i.e. $f(m)=m+n$.

So such a function exists. (Its values are $2,3,5,6,8,10,11,\dots$)

**Answer: Yes.**

imo-1993-06.title: A linear recurrence over $\mathbb{F}_2$
imo-1993-06.body:
Write $1$ for on and $0$ for off, and compute modulo $2$.

**Encoding.** Let $a_0=\dots=a_{n-1}=1$ be the initial states, and let $a_{i+n}$ be the state of $L_i$ just after step $s_i$. At step $s_i$ the lamp $L_i$ currently has the value $a_i$ and $L_{i-1}$ has the value $a_{i+n-1}$ (it was just set at step $s_{i-1}$; for $i=0$ this is the initial $a_{n-1}$). The rule "toggle $L_i$ iff $L_{i-1}$ is on" means
$$a_{i+n}=a_i+a_{i+n-1}\qquad(i\ge0).$$
After $M$ steps the lamps show the values $a_M,a_{M+1},\dots,a_{M+n-1}$ (the last value written to each lamp). So *all lamps are on after $M$ steps iff $a_M=\dots=a_{M+n-1}=1$*, i.e. iff the window of $n$ consecutive terms at position $M$ equals the window at position $0$. Since the recurrence determines everything from a window, this happens iff $a_{j+M}=a_j$ for all $j\ge0$.

**Generating function.** Let $A(x)=\sum_{j\ge0}a_jx^j\in\mathbb{F}_2[[x]]$ and $q(x)=1+x+x^n$. The coefficient of $x^j$ in $q(x)A(x)$ is $a_j+a_{j-1}+a_{j-n}$ (terms with negative index $=0$): it is $1$ for $j=0$, $1+1=0$ for $1\le j\le n-1$, and $0$ for $j\ge n$ by the recurrence. So $q(x)A(x)=1$.

**Criterion.** All lamps are on after $M$ steps $\iff$ $q(x)\mid 1+x^M$ in $\mathbb{F}_2[x]$.
Indeed, if $a_{j+M}=a_j$ for all $j$, then $(1+x^M)A(x)=P(x)$ is a polynomial, so $1+x^M=P(x)q(x)$. Conversely, if $1+x^M=P(x)q(x)$, then $(1+x^M)A(x)=P(x)$ has degree $M-n<M$, so the coefficient $a_j+a_{j-M}$ vanishes for all $j\ge M$.

Since $q(0)=1$, $x$ is invertible modulo $q$, so $q\mid1+x^M\iff x^M\equiv1$, and $q\mid x^r(1+x^M)\iff q\mid 1+x^M$.

**(a)** The ring $\mathbb{F}_2[x]/(q)$ is finite and $x$ is a unit in it, so some power $x^M$ ($M\ge1$) equals $1$. Then all lamps are on after $M$ steps.

**(b)** $n=2^k$. Modulo $q$ we have $x^n\equiv1+x$, and squaring is additive in characteristic $2$, so $(1+x)^{2^k}=1+x^{2^k}$. Hence
$$x^{n^2}=(x^n)^n\equiv(1+x)^n=1+x^n\equiv1+1+x=x .$$
So $q\mid x(x^{n^2-1}+1)$, hence $q\mid 1+x^{n^2-1}$: $M(n)=n^2-1$ works.

**(c)** $n=2^k+1$, write $m=2^k=n-1$. Modulo $q$:
$$x^{n^2}\equiv(1+x)^n=(1+x)^m(1+x)=(1+x^m)(1+x)=1+x+x^m+x^{n}\equiv 1+x+x^m+1+x=x^m .$$
So $q\mid x^m(x^{n^2-m}+1)$, hence $q\mid1+x^{n^2-n+1}$: $M(n)=n^2-n+1$ works. ∎
